title: Vendor context-switch interference bench
content:
Summary:

This doc captures an exploratory benchmark series that investigated tail-latency/throughput sensitivity when switching between short and long requests on different vendor GPUs and cloud SKUs. Motivation came from field reports (INC-2025) where customer workloads with a mix of short chat generation and long-context retrievals saw sudden p99 spikes after driver updates or VM type swaps. Aim was to reproduce, profile, and produce actionable knobs for the runtime.

High-level findings (raw):
- On A100 (p4d-equivalent) we saw a stable p50 but p99 amplifies by ~2.8x when short requests are interleaved with long-decoding requests compared to homogeneous short workloads.
- On H100 (hpc-optimized SKUs) the p99 amplification was lower (~1.6x) but throughput under mixed load dropped by ~18% relative to baseline.
- L40S (in Azure NDv5-like SKUs) exhibited the most variable behavior: some driver/CUDA combos produced dramatic p99 tails (4x) while others were close to H100 behavior.
- CUDA/driver interaction mattered: driver+CUDA 535.54 + CUDA 12.2 had lower kernel preemption overhead in our configs vs driver 520-series with CUDA 11.x.
- The dominant micro-root cause appears to be context-switch overhead combined with KV-cache eviction/restore work on long-token decodes; the runtime's kernel selection + CUDA stream scheduling amplifies this when the scheduler mixes synchronous short-launch work and long autoregressive kernels.

Test matrix (concise):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB, NVIDIA H100 80GB, NVIDIA L40S 48GB (public cloud SKU analogs: aws p4d, gcp h100, azure ndm_v5)
- Instances: 1-GPU and 8-GPU variants where applicable (we focused on single-GPU to isolate per-card behavior; small multi-GPU sanity checks done)
- Drivers/CUDA: 520.61 + CUDA 11.8, 525.xx + CUDA 11.8, 535.54 + CUDA 12.2
- Runtime: serving-runtime main @ commit 7b1f3e2 (profile hooks enabled, KV cache ON)
- Workloads: short-gen (prompt -> 40 tokens), long-gen (prompt -> 2048 tokens), mixed microworkload (80% short, 20% long interleaved in poisson pattern), steady long-only and short-only baselines
- Measurement: sustained 10-minute runs, 99th/95th/50th latency per token, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, kernel launch counts, context-switch counts (nsys + /proc metrics), NVLink/NVSwitch counters where available

Repro steps (short):
1) bootstrap instance image: Ubuntu 22.04, nvidia-driver (as noted), docker+nvidia-container-runtime
2) start serving-runtime with profiling flags: --profiling=nvtx --kv-cache=on --batching=on
3) run loadgen harness (loadgen/mix-run.py) with seed=20251106, poisson interarrival rates to target 800-1k short rps equivalent
4) collect nsys traces for 90s windows at 2m and 7m marks, pull /sys/class/kgsl (where applicable) and nvidia-smi pmon samples

Representative observations and profiles:
- A100 / driver 520 + CUDA 11.8: nsys traces show kernel preemption/queue flush events when long kernels start; short-kernel launches are delayed by up to 12ms at tail. Visible dips in SM utilization during the first 200 tokens of the long requests indicating cache warm-up + memory staging.
- H100 / driver 535 + CUDA 12.2: better pipelining of long kernels, shorter preemption stalls; however we observed longer latencies when concurrent housekeeping kernels (e.g., memory copies for KV checkpointing) were scheduled on the same stream.
- L40S: behavior was driver-dependent — with 525 series we saw excessive PCIe stall events in traces (likely driver-optimized paths falling back to PCIe transfers rather than NVLink staging). With 535+12.2 it improves, but still had higher variance than H100.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Kernel preemption and scheduler heuristics in older drivers cause large-tail amplification when mixing short and long workloads; newer drivers have improved heuristics and CUDA runtime changes which reduce the effect.
2) KV cache eviction/restore is effectively serialized with long decodes; eviction thrashing is worse on cards/firmware combos that have slower device <-> host transfer paths.
3) NUMA and PCIe locality (root complex placement) on some cloud SKUs introduces transient stalls when the runtime creates temporary host buffers for long requests.

Immediate mitigations we validated (cheap):
- Preferential stream partitioning: isolate short-gen work onto a dedicated CUDA stream and set the long-decode kernels to a lower priority stream where supported. This reduced observed p99 amplification by ~30% on A100 in our test.
- Dynamic batching gating: detect burst of short requests and apply fast-path (no KV checkpointing) to avoid unnecessary host-device copies. Risk: marginal quality/regeneration correctness tradeoffs — needs integration tests.
- Driver pinning recommendation: for critical clusters, pin to 535.54 + CUDA 12.2 (where validated) until further runtime mitigations land.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Multi-GPU coherence: how does NVLink/NVSwitch behavior change amplification when long requests run on different GPUs but share host-side batching queues? Need dedicated 8-GPU topology runs.
- Quantization interaction: do INT8/4 kernels change preemption timing materially? Early small tests show slightly smaller tails but not conclusive.
- Firmware (GPU BIOS/NVRAM) versions were held constant; vendor firmware deltas may matter for L40S—requesting SI/BIOS revisions from cloud partners.
- Does host page migration (hugepages vs default) affect eviction stalls? We saw small signals pointing to page-migration noise.

Action items (owners):
- (Maya) Run multi-GPU NVLink-connected mixed workload runs on H100 8x and A100 8x (target by 2025-12-01).
- (Diego) Add an e2e test in loadgen that toggles stream partitioning flags and reports p99 improvement (PR draft linked). Due 2025-11-28.
- (Priya) Coordinate with infra to pin driver 535.54 on the private test fleet and run a 24h soak to capture rare tail events. Due 2025-11-30.
- (Liam) File a vendor ticket with Azure for L40S oddity and collect firmware/BIOS from sampled instances. Jira INF-3241 assigned.

Notes on instrumentation pitfalls:
- nsys adds overhead; prefer sampling-based traces and complement with perf counters. During our runs we observed a 2-4% reduction in throughput under continuous tracing.
- /proc metrics for context-switch counts on the host are noisy; correlate with nvtx markers emitted at kernel boundaries for higher confidence.
- GPU power/thermal throttling can masquerade as scheduling noise. Ensure experiments use fresh instances and avoid background thermal ramp artifacts (cold-start each run).

Conclusion:
Mixed short/long workloads expose interaction effects between kernel scheduling, KV cache management, and host-device transfer topology. These effects are visible across A100/H100/L40S but magnitude and cause mix vary by driver/CUDA/firmware. Short-term wins include stream partitioning and driver pinning; longer-term requires runtime-level scheduling changes and vendor engagement for L40S anomalies.

Appendices (commands/snippets):
- Example nsys launch: 
  NSYS_PROFILE=1 nsys profile --output=mix-1 --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=1 --capture-range-end=2 python loadgen/mix-run.py --config mixed-small

- Example quick-check script (tail latency snapshot):
  python scripts/latency_snapshot.py --target http://localhost:8080/generate --qps 400 --duration 600 --pattern poisson --seed 2025

- Relevant tickets/threads:
  - JIRA INF-3241: L40S mixed-workload tail amplification
  - Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime "mixed load p99s after driver roll" (link above)

If you want raw traces (nsys archives) or CSV exports of the runs, we have the artifacts under gs://redwood-bench/vendor-context-switch-202511/ (access controlled) — see Diego for access.

Unresolved: decide whether to default stream-partitioning in runtime (risk: regressions for some legacy models) vs gating behind an opt-in flag for now. Suggest we opt-in and gather more canary telemetry before enabling globally.
